def-csm-frontier-finite-rate-process.definition_interface:
Fix a finite nonempty set of states $E$ and a finite time horizon $T\ge0$. A finite-state continuous-time Markov jump process on $[0,T]$ is a family of random elements $X_t$ with values in $E$ on a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$. Its paths are constant between successive jump times and take the new state at a jump time (right-continuity); path events use the sigma-algebra generated by the coordinate maps $X_t$. The Markov property here means that, conditional on the history through time $s$, the law of the future path depends on that history only through $(s,X_s)$. For each pair of distinct states $x,y\in E$, its transition rate $\kappa_{xy}:[0,T]\to[0,\infty)$ is a bounded continuous function. Write

$$\lambda_x(t):=\sum_{y\in E,\ y\ne x}\kappa_{xy}(t).$$

All time integrals without a displayed measure below are oriented Riemann integrals. When a continuous integrand is used as a Lebesgue density, its Lebesgue and Riemann integrals agree by the bounded Riemann-integral comparison theorem. The first-jump rate convention is the following. Conditional on the process history through time $s$ and state $X_s=x$, the survival probability of no jump before time $t$, $s\le t\le T$, is

$$H_x(s,t):=\exp\left(-\int_s^t\lambda_x(u)\,du\right).$$

For each $y\ne x$, the conditional density that the next jump occurs at time $t$ and goes to $y$ is $H_x(s,t)\kappa_{xy}(t)$ with respect to one-dimensional Lebesgue measure; the remaining probability $H_x(s,T)$ is that no jump occurs by time $T$. These are normalized conditional probabilities: for $s<T$, by the chain rule and the first fundamental theorem of calculus, $H_x(s,s)=1$ and $H'_x(s,t)=-\lambda_x(t)H_x(s,t)$; the density integrands are continuous, so

$$H_x(s,T)+\sum_{y\ne x}\int_s^T H_x(s,t)\kappa_{xy}(t)\,dt =H_x(s,T)+\int_s^T\lambda_x(t)H_x(s,t)\,dt=1.$$

After each jump the same conditional rule restarts from the new state and jump time. For $s=T$, the next-jump law has unit mass on no further jump. The row generator is the matrix $Q(t)$ with $Q_{xy}(t)=\kappa_{xy}(t)$ for $x\ne y$ and $Q_{xx}(t)=-\lambda_x(t)$. A time-homogeneous process is the special case in which every $\kappa_{xy}(t)$ is constant. When rates carry physical time units, $\kappa_{xy}$ has units of inverse time; this definition is mathematical and asserts no physical realization. The process is called nonexplosive on $[0,T]$ when its path has finitely many jumps there almost surely.

derivations.claim: Conditional on state $x_0$ at time $0$, the first-jump convention in [F1] gives the survival factor $H_{x_0}(0,t_1)$ and jump density $H_{x_0}(0,t_1)\kappa_{x_0x_1}(t_1)$. After this jump, the Markov rule restarts at $x_1$. Multiplying the successive conditional survival and jump factors through state $x_n$, and then the final no-jump survival on $[t_n,T]$, gives exactly the stated path density. If $n=0$, the same convention gives $\rho(x_0)H_{x_0}(0,T)$, which is the stated boundary formula.

Let $J=[s,t]$ have length $\delta$ with $M\delta<1$. The density of the first $n$ ordered jumps, with survival factors removed, is at most the product of the $n$ rates. Summing these products over each successive state gives at most $M^n$. The ordered time simplex is contained in the cube $J^n$, whose Lebesgue volume is $\delta^n$ by [F2]. Hence $\mathbb P(N_J\ge n)\le(M\delta)^n$. Pointwise $N_J=\sum_{n\ge1}\mathbf 1_{\{N_J\ge n\}}$; [F4] gives $\mathbb E[N_J]\le\sum_{n\ge1}(M\delta)^n=M\delta/(1-M\delta)$.

If $T=0$ or $M=0$, there are no jumps. Otherwise choose a positive integer $m>MT$ by [F3] and partition $[0,T]$ into $m$ intervals of length $\delta=T/m$, so $M\delta<1$. Jump times have densities by step 1.1, hence no jump occurs at a fixed partition endpoint with positive probability. The total count is the sum of the interval counts almost surely; linearity of expectation [F4] and step 1.2 give $\mathbb E[N_T]\le mM\delta/(1-M\delta)<\infty$. If $\mathbb P(N_T=\infty)>0$, then $\mathbb E[N_T]\ge n\mathbb P(N_T=\infty)$ for every $n$, contradicting finiteness. Thus the process is nonexplosive and the countable path-density collection covers the path law.

def-csm-frontier-stationary-path-entropy.definition_interface:
Let $E$ be a finite nonempty state set, let $q_{xy}\ge0$ be finite time-homogeneous transition rates for distinct $x,y\in E$, and let $Q$ be their row generator. Let $\pi$ be a strictly positive probability row vector with $\pi Q=0$; the forward-equation theorem shows that this is a stationary law when used initially. Assume symmetric support: $q_{xy}>0$ if and only if $q_{yx}>0$. For a sample path on a finite interval $[0,T]$ with successive jump states $x_0,x_1,\ldots,x_n$, define its stationary path entropy by

$$S_T:=\sum_{j=1}^n\log\left(\frac{\pi_{x_{j-1}}q_{x_{j-1}x_j}}{\pi_{x_j}q_{x_jx_{j-1}}}\right).$$

The bounded-rate path-density lemma shows that the process is nonexplosive on every finite horizon. Thus the sum is finite almost surely; set $S_T=0$ on the null exceptional set of paths with infinitely many jumps. Its Borel preimages are countable unions of measurable path strata indexed by jump number and finite state sequence, so $S_T$ is a real random variable. The empty sum for a path with no jumps is $0$. Every logarithm is defined because $\pi_x>0$ and symmetric support makes both rates in each jump ratio positive. The quantity $S_T$ is dimensionless and depends only on the ordered jump states, not on their times. Detailed balance with respect to $\pi$ means $\pi_xq_{xy}=\pi_yq_{yx}$ for every pair $x\ne y$; under this condition each jump contribution is zero, but no detailed-balance condition is part of this definition.

derivations.claim: On the canonical path space, write a path with $n$ jumps as its state sequence and ordered jump times. Its jump count is $$N_{xy}(T)=\sum_{j=1}^n\mathbf 1_{\{x_{j-1}=x,\ x_j=y\}}.$$ Using the nonnegative path densities [F2], the expectation is the sum over $n\ge1$, state sequences, and ordered jump-time simplices of this count times the path density. The state-sequence sums are finite at each $n$, and their union over $n$ is countable; the increasing partial sums and [F3] justify the countable sum. For each fixed $n$ and jump index $j$, write the ordered-time simplex integral as an integral over $[0,T]^n$ with its simplex indicator. This is a nonnegative measurable function: the factors are continuous rates and survival functions, and the simplex is Borel. Lebesgue measure on the cube is finite and counting measure on the finite state sequences is finite, so [F4] permits integrating first in the selected jump time $s=t_j$ and then summing the other times. Summing over $n$ and $j$ is again an increasing nonnegative sum, so [A1] and [F3] justify its rearrangement.

For each selected jump at time $s$, the Markov property factors its path density into the prefix density through state $x$, the transition factor $\kappa_{xy}(s)\,ds$, and the suffix density starting in $y$. At fixed $s$, all finite prefixes ending in $x$ partition $\{X_s=x\}$ up to the null event of a jump at the fixed time $s$, so their densities sum to $p_x(s)$. All finite suffix densities starting in $y$ sum to $1$ by the normalization and nonexplosion conclusion of [F2]. The nonnegative sum/integral interchange justified in step 1.1 therefore gives the Lebesgue integral $\int_{[0,T]}p_x(s)\kappa_{xy}(s)\,d\lambda_1(s)$.

Conditional on $X_s=x$, the probability of at least one jump by time $t>s$ is $1-H_x(s,t)=1-e^{-u}$ with $u:=\int_s^t\lambda_x(r)\,dr\ge0$. The inequality $1-e^{-u}\le u$ and the rate bound give this probability at most $M(t-s)$, uniformly in $x$. Hence $|p_x(t)-p_x(s)|\le\mathbb P(X_t\ne X_s)\le M|t-s|$, so each $p_x$ is continuous. The product $p_x(t)\kappa_{xy}(t)$ is consequently continuous and bounded on $[0,T]$, so its Lebesgue integral is finite. If $T>0$, [F5] identifies that integral with the Riemann integral in the Statement. If $T=0$, both the count and integral are zero by [F6]. This proves the identity for every $T\ge0$.

By [F4], a clockwise jump $i\to i+1$ contributes $\log((\pi_i a)/(\pi_{i+1}b))=\log(a/b)$, while a counterclockwise jump contributes $\log((\pi_i b)/(\pi_{i-1}a))=-\log(a/b)$. Summing over all jumps gives $S_T=(N_+-N_-)\log(a/b)$, including the no-jump case when both counts are zero.

Detailed balance on an edge requires $\pi_i a=\pi_{i+1}b$, which under the uniform law is equivalent to $a=b$. If $a=b$, this equality holds on every edge; nonedges have zero rate in both directions. Hence detailed balance holds exactly in the symmetric-rate case.

By [F3] and stationarity from step 1.1, $$\mathbb E[N_+]=\sum_i\mathbb E[N_{i,i+1}] =\sum_i\int_0^T\frac1N a\,dt=aT,\qquad \mathbb E[N_-]=\sum_i\mathbb E[N_{i,i-1}] =\sum_i\int_0^T\frac1N b\,dt=bT.$$ Thus step 1.2 gives $\mathbb E[S_T]=(aT-bT)\log(a/b)=T(a-b)\log(a/b)$. Since $\log$ is strictly increasing by [F6], $a-b$ and $\log(a/b)$ have the same sign, so their product is nonnegative.

The ring is irreducible because both rates are positive and repeated clockwise jumps connect every pair of states. It has positive stationary law $\pi$ and symmetric support because every edge has both rates positive. Therefore [F5] applies and gives the stated exact finite-time fluctuation relation, with no assumption of a probability density for $S_T$.
